attachment.content:
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

content.content: {"result":"{\"success\": true, \"data\": {\"path\": \"/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-be-idea-gen-0519-3/projects/irt_personfit_contam/paper_framing.md\", \"content\": \"# Paper Framing — irt_personfit_contam\\n\\n## Target Venue\\n- Primary: EMNLP 2026 Main (用户确认；ARR submission DDL 5/25 — 需确认可行性)\\n- Fallback: AAAI 2027 (abstract 7/21, full paper 7/28, ~10 weeks)\\n- Backup: ICLR 2027 (~Sep 2026, ~17 weeks)\\n\\n## Core Reframe (D031, 2026-05-21)\\n\\n**旧 narrative**: \\\"ℓz* 作为 LLM contamination 检测工具\\\"\\n**新 narrative**: \\\"首次系统刻画 IRT person-fit 在 LLM benchmark contamination 检测中的行为边界\\\"\\n\\n贡献不是 \\\"提出检测方法\\\"，而是 \\\"回答: binary response patterns 能检测到什么？在什么条件下？什么条件下失效？\\\" 这是 characterization paper, 不是 tool paper。\\n\\n## Core Claims (3 条, n=10 updated)\\n\\n**Claim 1 (Boundary Conditions of IRT Person-Fit for Contamination Detection)**:\\nIRT person-fit statistics detect SFT contamination with large effect sizes across three model families and two benchmarks (all 8 Cohen's d CIs exclude zero, n=10 per condition). However, detection power is modulated by boundary conditions that we systematically characterize: (a) **θ-shift absorption** — contamination raises θ_MLE, and high-baseline-accuracy models (Qwen 83%) absorb more signal (d_50=1.08) than low-baseline models (Llama 59%, d_50=2.50); (b) **inverted-U dose-response** — under free-θ estimation, Qwen shows non-monotonic detection (d_15=4.83 > d_50=1.08), while z-score increases monotonically; (c) **benchmark size × θ-boundary interaction** — ARC-C (295 items) shows d_50=5.30 vs MMLU d_50=1.08 due to θ estimation ceiling effects. The **detection-diagnosis tradeoff**: z-score |d| >> HT |d| ≥ lz* |d| (Qwen 15%: z=42, HT=7.3, lz*=4.8). Simpler statistics detect more powerfully, but only lz* enables diagnostic characterization (seen/unseen decomposition, θ-shift mechanism, inverted-U). HT also exhibits inverted-U (Qwen HT d_15=7.3 >> d_50=1.7), confirming θ-shift absorption affects all person-fit statistics. **Post-RL (D033/D034)**: GRPO training erases accuracy-based signal (seen/unseen gap 11pp→0.2pp) but ℓz* pattern gap persists (~3.3) — a hard boundary for accuracy-based methods with residual structure in response patterns. N=1 model (Qwen), caveat in Limitations.\\n\\n**Claim 2 (Detection Characterization + Baselines)**:\\nDetection power follows an empirical power function with benchmark size (R²=0.65, upper bound). ARC-C (295 items) validates cross-benchmark applicability. **Degradation chain baseline comparison**: at detection level, HT (difficulty-only) matches ℓz* (full 4PL); accuracy z-score also detects in controlled settings (z=56.7 at contam_50). But z-score cannot capture inverted-U (monotonically increases), seen/unseen decomposition, or θ-shift mechanism. ℓz*'s unique value: (i) parametric null ≈N(0,1) enables direct hypothesis testing; (ii) Snijders correction compensates θ estimation error; (iii) 4-parameter item weighting handles cross-subject heterogeneity. Item-level detection near-random for ALL binary methods (AUROC 0.52–0.63) — contamination signal is diffuse, model-level aggregation essential.\\n\\n**Claim 3 (Empirical Findings from Real LLM Data)**:\\n(a) **Universal 4PL model misfit** — 57/60 cells flagged (|lz*| >> 5), LLM response patterns fundamentally violate IRT assumptions. Motivates Δlz* design. (b) **Cross-family baseline divergence** — clean lz* spans ~9σ (Qwen +8.28, Mistral +5.42, Llama -0.14), precluding absolute threshold detection. Relative detection (Δlz*/Cohen's d) is essential. (c) **PSN-IRT 12-model case study** with validated 4PL parameters.\\n\\n## Story Spine\\n\\n**Problem**: Benchmark contamination undermines LLM evaluation reliability. As benchmarks proliferate and training corpora grow, contamination risk increases, but all existing detection methods require privileged access — training data (n-gram overlap), token probabilities (Min-K%, MIA), model weights (internal probing), or specially crafted prompts (Time Travel). A contaminated LLM is functionally analogous to an examinee with item preknowledge, yet no work has connected the mature psychometric literature on cheating detection to LLM benchmark integrity.\\n\\n**Existing approaches & gaps**: Detection methods circa 2026 span five families: time-based partition, MIA/Min-K%++ (ICLR 2024), Time Travel probing (ICLR 2024 Spotlight), ConStat performance-based testing (NeurIPS 2024), and CoDeC in-context learning effects (ICLR 2026). Wang et al. (2025) show all MIA-based methods fail under post-RL contamination. ## Core Claims (3 条, n=10 updated)

**Claim 1 (Boundary Conditions of IRT Person-Fit for Contamination Detection)**:
IRT person-fit statistics detect SFT contamination with large effect sizes across three model families and two benchmarks (all 8 Cohen's d CIs exclude zero, n=10 per condition). However, detection power is modulated by boundary conditions that we systematically characterize: (a) **θ-shift absorption** — contamination raises θ_MLE, and high-baseline-accuracy models (Qwen 83%) absorb more signal (d_50=1.08) than low-baseline models (Llama 59%, d_50=2.50); (b) **inverted-U dose-response** — under free-θ estimation, Qwen shows non-monotonic detection (d_15=4.83 > d_50=1.08), while z-score increases monotonically; (c) **benchmark size × θ-boundary interaction** — ARC-C (295 items) shows d_50=5.30 vs MMLU d_50=1.08 due to θ estimation ceiling effects. **Claim 2 (Detection Characterization + Baselines)**:
Detection power follows an empirical power function with benchmark size (R²=0.65, upper bound). Item-level detection near-random for ALL binary methods (AUROC 0.52–0.63) — contamination signal is diffuse, model-level aggregation essential.

**Claim 3 (Empirical Findings from Real LLM Data)**:
(a) **Universal 4PL model misfit** — 57/60 cells flagged (|lz*| >> 5), LLM response patterns fundamentally violate IRT assumptions. Motivates Δlz* design. (b) **Cross-family baseline divergence** — clean lz* spans ~9σ (Qwen +8.28, Mistral +5.42, Llama -0.14), precluding absolute threshold detection. Relative detection (Δlz*/Cohen's d) is essential. (c) **PSN-IRT 12-model case study** with validated 4PL parameters.

## Story Spine

**Problem**: Benchmark contamination undermines LLM evaluation reliability. As benchmarks proliferate and training corpora grow, contamination risk increases, but all existing detection methods require privileged access — training data (n-gram overlap), token probabilities (Min-K%, MIA), model weights (internal probing), or specially crafted prompts (Time Travel). A contaminated LLM is functionally analogous to an examinee with item preknowledge, yet no work has connected the mature psychometric literature on cheating detection to LLM benchmark integrity.

**Existing approaches & gaps**: Detection methods circa 2026 span five families: time-based partition, MIA/Min-K%++ (ICLR 2024), Time Travel probing (ICLR 2024 Spotlight), ConStat performance-based testing (NeurIPS 2024), and CoDeC in-context learning effects (ICLR 2026). Wang et al. (2025) show all MIA-based methods fail under post-RL contamination. Critically, ALL require more than binary response patterns — no method operates at the minimal-information level.

**Our framing**: We establish the minimal-information operating point on the contamination detection frontier. By repurposing IRT person-fit statistics — developed over decades for detecting exam cheating — we ask: "What can be detected from binary response patterns alone?" We show: (1) in simulation, person-fit statistics achieve high detection power (97.9% on MMLU-scale benchmarks) with well-calibrated null distributions; (2) in real LLM data, response patterns universally deviate from 4PL predictions — the statistical framework is sound, but LLMs genuinely violate IRT assumptions (local independence, unidimensionality), producing extreme lz* values across nearly all models; (3) controlled contamination experiments leverage this by measuring Δlz* between clean and contaminated models — since the null is well-calibrated, within-model shifts are statistically interpretable. The universal model misfit finding is itself a contribution — it reveals that LLM response patterns are fundamentally different from classical test-taker patterns.

10. **Validation hierarchy** — ctrl-contam = primary validation (ground truth, same model clean vs contaminated); 12-model case study = empirical findings (no ground truth, but validated parameters); v1 data = future work roadmap. Paper structure should reflect this priority.
9. **lz* measures memorization, not generalization** — lz* detects aberrant patterns (memorization signature), not smooth ability improvement (generalization). This is a feature: it distinguishes genuine learning from rote memorization. Power function gives upper bound; ctrl-contam measures actual memorization fraction.
10. **Negative results as contributions** — D007 (universal misfit) and D008 (empirical null well-calibrated) are "honest negative results that become positive contributions": universal misfit is a novel finding about LLM response patterns; the simulation-reality gap motivates Δlz* and quantifies SFT generalization. D011 (MML-EM refit failure) is a methodological caveat (classical vs neural IRT sample requirements). D009 (item alignment) is a data engineering detail (1 sentence in Data section). Present negatives with the framing: "the gap between where IRT works perfectly (simulation) and where it struggles (real LLM data) is itself informative."
11. **ctrl-contam actual results (D015)** — contam_15 |d|=3.85 (strong), contam_50 non-monotonic under free-θ but **monotonic under θ-fixed** (ratio=2.93). θ-shift is the mechanism: contamination→higher θ_MLE→absorbs aberrance signal. Frame as "principled detection with quantified operating characteristics + θ-shift boundary condition." Headline: "We don't just detect — we characterize, including the conditions under which detection degrades." Do NOT claim "state-of-the-art detection."
12. **θ-shift as methodological contribution (D015)** — Person-fit sensitivity degrades when θ is re-estimated on contaminated data. This is a novel finding for contamination detection: (a) θ-fixed analysis recovers monotonic dose-response, (b) the θ-shift magnitude (0.47 at 50% contamination) quantifies the confound, (c) practical implication: use pre-contamination θ baseline or cross-validated θ. Present as a contribution, not a limitation.
13. **Cross-family baseline lz* divergence (Reviewer WARNING)** — Clean lz* spans ~9σ: Qwen +8.68, Mistral +5.42, Llama -0.14. 固定阈值检测失效（Qwen contam_15 lz*=+3.85 仍为正值）。论文必须：(a) 明确 IRT-FIT 是相对检测（Δlz*/Cohen's d），非绝对阈值；(b) 展示 clean baseline lz* 跨家族差异表；(c) 预防性回答"contam_15 lz*=+3.85 为正值为何算污染"（因为 Δlz*=-4.83 是大效应）；(d) lz* baseline 作为"模型内部一致性"指标——Mistral acc 最低(0.514)但 lz* 第二高(+5.42)，说明 lz* 捕捉 difficulty-ordering 一致性而非准确率。
14. **Inverted-U 是模型相关的** — Qwen 在 15%→50% 区间出现强 inversion（Δlz* 50%=-1.39 << 15%=-4.83），Llama 和 Mistral 在此区间 Δlz* 单调增大。Inverted-U 在 free-θ 下由 baseline misfit 调制——高 baseline lz* (Qwen +8.68) 的模型更容易出现 non-monotonicity。论文不能 claim inverted-U 为 universal phenomenon，需加 model-dependent caveat。θ-fixed 分析仍恢复所有家族的 monotonicity — 这是 θ-fixed 贡献的关键证据。
15. **seen/unseen split as strongest signal** — contam_15 seen lz*≈0 (memorized items look "normal") vs unseen lz*=3.1. This is the clearest contamination fingerprint: items that should produce aberrant responses instead produce expected responses. More interpretable than aggregate Δlz*.

## Writing Strategy (from Distillation)

- **Story type**: "跨界迁移型" — unused in 0/8 peer papers. Our unique angle.
- **Figure 1**: Problem illustration (dual-panel: contaminated vs clean response pattern). Use psychometric hook — impossible response pattern (hard items right, easy wrong).
- **Contribution structure**: 3 contributions (method + characterization + empirical findings), escalating scope. Standard in 5/8 papers.
- **Result tables**: Row=methods, col=datasets×metrics. Bold-best. Average column.
- **Numbered findings**: Adopt PSN-IRT's "Key Discoveries" strategy for scannable presentation.
- **CIs as differentiator**: 6/8 peer papers report no variance. Our bootstrap CIs are a competitive advantage.
- **Baseline count**: Peer median ~5. Target ≥5 baselines.

## Evidence Summary

- **Phase A (simulation)**: Null check passed (4PL compatible with lz* theory). MMLU power@15%=97.9%. Power ∝ n_items confirmed. Simulation results stand — they establish theoretical detection capacity within the 4PL model.
- **Phase B (real data)**: Gemini-1.5 MMLU acc=1.000, θ=0.78, lz*=+31.81. Cross-benchmark anomaly profiles identified.
- **Empirical null analysis (exp-empirical-null)**: Bootstrap null calibration is benchmark-size dependent — large benchmarks well-calibrated (MMLU: mean bias 0.041, std 1.003, KS reject 8.3%; HellaSwag: 8.3%), small benchmarks poorly calibrated (HumanEval: 75%, ARC-C: 58.3%; overall KS reject 40%, 24/60). The statistical framework is sound for large benchmarks (n>10K). 57/60 real-data cells flagged because LLM lz* values are genuinely extreme (|lz*| >> 5) — this reflects **universal 4PL model misfit** (LLM response patterns violate IRT assumptions), not contamination-specific detection. **Important**: 57/60 vs accuracy z-score 4/60 demonstrates lz* captures response-pattern information beyond aggregate accuracy (evidence for Claim 3a universal misfit), NOT contamination detection superiority. Contamination detection evidence comes from simulation (lz* AUROC 0.675 vs ML 0.575 at 5%) and ctrl-contam (d=3.42, n=3, ddof=1, ℓz*-corrected).
- **Calibration gap reframed (D007→D008)**: The gap is not "null is biased" but "real LLM data genuinely deviates from 4PL". This strengthens Δlz* approach: well-calibrated null means within-model shifts are statistically meaningful.
- **Controlled contamination — FINAL n=10 data (2026-05-21 recalculated, Snijders-corrected)**:

  | Model | Benchmark | d(15%) | 95% CI | d(50%) | 95% CI |
  |-------|-----------|--------|--------|--------|--------|
  | Qwen 2.5-7B | MMLU | 4.83 | [2.94, 14.29] | 1.08 | [0.30, 3.93] |
  | Llama 3.1-8B | MMLU | 2.27 | [1.56, 4.63] | 2.50 | [1.76, 5.19] |
  | Mistral 7B v0.3 | MMLU | 2.64 | [1.49, 7.38] | 3.50 | [2.09, 9.59] |
  | Qwen 2.5-7B | ARC-C | 3.16 | [2.01, 9.54] | 5.30 | [3.64, 15.49] |

  All 8 CIs exclude zero. **Qwen contam_50 CI [0.30, 3.93] — lower bound near zero due to inverted-U (θ-shift absorption). Must be honestly reported + θ-fixed analysis presented as remedy.**

  Key patterns: (a) Qwen inverted-U (d_15=4.83 > d_50=1.08), Llama/Mistral monotonic (d_50 > d_15); (b) θ-shift absorption modulated by baseline accuracy (Qwen 83% >> Llama 59%); (c) ARC-C d_50=5.30 >> MMLU d_50=1.08 (benchmark size × θ-boundary); (d) Degradation chain: HT achieves |d| within 0.3 of ℓz*, z-score also detects (z=56.7 at contam_50).

  **Note**: n=10 recalculation changed values from earlier n=3 reports (e.g., Qwen d_15 was 3.42→4.83 due to Snijders correction factor recalculation with 10 seeds). Registry n=10 version is authoritative.

- **GRPO Post-RL (D033/D034)**: Qwen 2.5-7B, GRPO after SFT contamination.
  - acc_seen: 83.1% → 73.0% → 73.1% → 73.2% (step 0/500/1000/1500)
  - acc_unseen: 73.1% (stable) → gap erased by step 500
  - ℓz* seen/unseen gap: 3.67 → 3.59 → 3.32 (pattern persists after accuracy erasure)
  - **Conclusion**: accuracy-based detection = hard boundary post-RL; pattern-level structure persists. N=1 model, Limitations caveat.

- **z-score baseline (D032)**: z-score detects contamination in ctrl-contam (z=56.7 at contam_50, trivially significant). BUT: z-score monotonically increases with contamination dose, cannot capture inverted-U phenomenon. Confirms degradation chain at detection level; ℓz* value is characterization, not detection.

- **4PL real-data degradation**: 3PL(d=1) vs 4PL lz* correlation r=0.225, RMSE=68.41. d parameter essential for high-ability models (DeepSeek-V3 Δ=357). Complements simulation ablation (+14-27pp power gain).

1	\section{Results}
2	\label{sec:results}
3	
4	\subsection{Detection Signal Across Model Families}
5	\label{sec:detection}
6	
7	Table~\ref{tab:cohens_d} presents Cohen's $d$ effect sizes for $\ell_z^*$ across three model families and two benchmarks.
8	All confidence intervals exclude zero, confirming that $\Delta\ell_z^*$ reliably separates contaminated from clean models at both contamination levels.
9	
10	On MMLU, effect sizes range from $|d|{=}1.99$ (Llama at 25\%) to $|d|{=}7.44$ (Qwen at 25\%), with Qwen at 5\% ($|d|{=}4.15$) confirming detection at the lowest contamination level tested. Llama ($|d|{=}2.11$/$1.99$/$2.33$) and Mistral ($|d|{=}3.01$/$3.50$) show comparable magnitudes.
11	On ARC-C (295 items), Qwen yields $|d|{=}3.16$ at 15\% and $|d|{=}5.30$ at 50\%, demonstrating that detection remains feasible even on small benchmarks when contamination is sufficiently concentrated.
12	
13	Clean-model $\ell_z^*$ baselines diverge substantially across families: Qwen ${+}8.68$ ($\text{SD}{=}0.74$), Mistral ${+}4.02$ ($\text{SD}{=}2.05$), Llama ${+}0.26$ ($\text{SD}{=}1.54$), and ARC-C Qwen ${-}5.42$ ($\text{SD}{=}0.16$).
14	Absolute $\ell_z^*$ thresholds would produce contradictory results: Qwen's contaminated $\ell_z^*$ at 15\% (${+}3.8$) is still positive.
15	The $\Delta\ell_z^*$ design normalizes these divergent baselines: Cohen's $d$ yields comparable effect sizes ($|d|{=}1.99$--$7.44$) despite order-of-magnitude differences.
16	Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} provides a visual summary.
17	
18	\begin{table}[t]
19	\centering
20	\caption{Cohen's $d$ for $\Delta\ell_z^*$ across model families ($n{=}10$ clean seeds). Single-seed conditions: percentile bootstrap 95\% CI (10,000 resamples) reflecting clean-seed variability. Qwen MMLU 15\%/25\%/50\%: multi-seed mean $\pm$ SD ($n{=}3$ independent contamination runs). All 95\% CIs exclude zero.}
21	\label{tab:cohens_d}
22	\footnotesize
23	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
24	\begin{tabular}{@{}llrrrr@{}}
25	\toprule
26	Model & Bench. & $d$ (5\%) [CI] & $d$ (15\%) [CI] & $d$ (25\%) [CI] & $d$ (50\%) [CI] \\
27	\midrule
28	Qwen$^{\dagger}$ & MMLU & $-4.15$ [$-9.9$, $-2.7$] & $-5.36$ ($\pm$1.10) & $-7.44$ ($\pm$1.86) & $-5.08$ ($\pm$3.02) \\
29	Llama & MMLU & --- & $-2.11$ [$-4.8$, $-1.4$] & $-1.99$ [$-4.4$, $-1.3$] & $-2.33$ [$-5.1$, $-1.6$] \\
30	Mistral & MMLU & --- & $-3.01$ [$-8.2$, $-1.8$] & --- & $-3.50$ [$-9.4$, $-2.1$] \\
31	Qwen$^{\dagger}$ & ARC-C & --- & $+3.16$ [$2.0$, $9.5$] & --- & $+5.30$ [$3.6$, $15.2$] \\
32	\bottomrule
33	\multicolumn{6}{@{}l}{\scriptsize $^{\dagger}$15\%/25\%/50\%: multi-seed means ($n{=}3$ QLoRA runs); 5\%: single seed. Per-seed values in Appendix~\ref{app:reproducibility}.}
34	\end{tabular}}
35	\end{table}
36	
37	\begin{figure*}[t]
38	  \centering
39	  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_heatmap.pdf}
40	  \caption{Cohen's $|d|$ heatmap (single-seed values; multi-seed means in Table~\ref{tab:cohens_d}). Blue intensity reflects effect-size magnitude. Grey cells: conditions not tested. Rows indicate model families; columns indicate contamination levels on MMLU (left) and ARC-C (right).}
41	  \label{fig:heatmap}
42	\end{figure*}
43	
44	\subsection{Model-Specific $\theta$-Shift Dynamics}
45	\label{sec:theta_dynamics}
46	
47	The cross-family variation in Table~\ref{tab:cohens_d}---Qwen's $|d|$ declining from 25\% to 50\% while Llama's remains flat---suggests detection sensitivity depends on more than contamination dose.
48	Contamination raises overall accuracy, which inflates $\hat{\theta}_{\text{MLE}}$; a higher $\hat{\theta}$ ``explains away'' anomalous successes on hard items, absorbing the contamination signal into the ability estimate.
49	We term this \emph{$\theta$-shift absorption}.
50	The magnitude of $\theta$-shift is comparable across families---Qwen ($\Delta\theta{=}0.47$ at 50\%) and Llama ($\Delta\theta{=}0.52$)---yet their fixed-$\theta$ amplification diverges markedly (Table~\ref{tab:theta_fixed}), indicating that $\theta$-shift magnitude alone does not predict fixed-$\theta$ benefit.
51	Figure~\ref{fig:theta_scatter} plots baseline accuracy against Cohen's $|d|$ for all model-benchmark combinations.
52	
53	$\theta$-shift absorption is the dominant source of detection variability for high-ability models at high contamination:
54	(i) fixed-$\theta$ estimation amplifies Qwen's multi-seed $|d|$ by 2.4$\times$ at 50\% ($5.08 \to 12.32$; Table~\ref{tab:theta_fixed}), while Llama shows no amplification ($0.4\times$);
55	(ii) $\theta$-anchoring reduces Qwen's inter-seed CV from 60\% to 19\%, confirming that training-run variance is driven by $\theta$-shift stochasticity rather than true signal variance;
56	(iii) the cross-model ranking under free-$\theta$ is seed-dependent at 50\%, making $\theta$-anchoring a necessary condition for reliable detection of high-ability models at high contamination.
57	
58	ARC-C reverses this pattern.
59	Despite Qwen's high baseline accuracy on ARC-C (89.7\%), contamination produces larger, not smaller, effect sizes ($|d|{=}3.16$ at 15\%, $|d|{=}5.30$ at 50\%).
60	This reversal reflects a ceiling effect: with only 295 items and 89.7\% baseline accuracy, the already-correct items offer minimal room for further $\theta$ inflation, so contamination manifests primarily as anomalous successes on the few remaining hard items.
61	The small item count amplifies this concentration, producing a disproportionately large $\ell_z^*$ shift per contaminated item.
62	
63	The baseline $\ell_z^*$ for ARC-C is negative ($-5.42$), reflecting the 4PL model's expectation of near-perfect performance; contamination pushes $\ell_z^*$ toward zero, producing the positive Cohen's $d$ values in Table~\ref{tab:cohens_d}.
64	
65	These findings indicate that detection sensitivity is not a fixed property of $\ell_z^*$ but depends on the interaction between model ability and benchmark characteristics, a consideration absent from standard person-fit applications.
66	
67	\paragraph{Fixed-$\theta$ estimation.}
68	Table~\ref{tab:theta_fixed} compares free-$\theta$ and fixed-$\theta$ Cohen's $d$ across all three families.
69	The benefit of fixed-$\theta$ is modulated by baseline $\ell_z^*$ level rather than $\theta$-shift magnitude.
70	Qwen (67.8\% accuracy, $\Delta\theta{=}0.47$, baseline $\ell_z^*{=}{+}8.68$) shows 2.4$\times$ amplification at 50\%: its large baseline departure from the IRT null provides substantial signal that free-$\theta$ absorption erodes, which $\theta$-anchoring recovers (multi-seed mean ${\ell_z^*}_{\text{fixed}} {=} 14.5$ vs.\ clean $7.35$).
71	Mistral (52.4\%, baseline $\ell_z^*{=}{+}4.02$) shows 1.7$\times$ at 50\%.
72	Llama (59.4\%, $\Delta\theta{=}0.39$ at 15\%, $0.52$ at 50\%) shows 0.4$\times$ at 50\% despite comparable $\theta$-shift: its near-zero baseline $\ell_z^*$ ($+0.26$) indicates that the clean response pattern conforms to IRT expectations, leaving no absorbed signal for $\theta$-anchoring to recover.
73	The amplification ratio tracks baseline $|\ell_z^*|$ monotonically ($8.68 {\to} 2.4{\times}$; $4.02 {\to} 1.7{\times}$; $0.26 {\to} 0.4{\times}$ at 50\%), making fixed-$\theta$ a targeted remedy for models with substantial baseline misfit, not a universal one.
74	
75	\begin{table}[t]
76	\centering
77	\caption{Free-$\theta$ vs.\ fixed-$\theta$ Cohen's $|d|$ on MMLU (bootstrap 95\% CI). Fixed-$\theta$ anchors $\hat{\theta}$ at the clean-model mean, eliminating $\theta$-shift absorption.}

91	Mistral$^{\ddagger}$ & 3.01 & 2.69 & 0.9$\times$ & [1.53, 9.06] \\

108	  \label{fig:theta_scatter}
109	\end{figure}

111	\subsection{Detection-Diagnosis Tradeoff}
112	\label{sec:degradation}
113	
114	Having established that $\theta$-shift complicates detection, we ask whether the full 4PL framework is necessary, or whether simpler statistics suffice.
115	Table~\ref{tab:degradation} compares three statistics at decreasing levels of information access: $\ell_z^*$ (requires 4PL parameters $a, b, c, d$), the HT statistic (requires only difficulty $b$), and an accuracy $z$-score (requires no item parameters).
116	
117	The comparison reveals a detection-diagnosis tradeoff.
118	For pure detection, simpler statistics are more powerful: accuracy $z$-scores yield $|d|$ values several-fold to over an order of magnitude larger than person-fit statistics (Table~\ref{tab:degradation}), because cross-seed accuracy variance is near-zero in controlled settings.
119	HT generally exceeds $\ell_z^*$ in detection strength, since HT is not attenuated by the Snijders correction for $\theta$ estimation uncertainty.
120	Both person-fit statistics exhibit seed-dependent non-monotonicity under free-$\theta$ estimation (Table~\ref{tab:degradation}), confirming that $\theta$-shift absorption affects all statistics conditioned on ability, not $\ell_z^*$ specifically.
121	
122	Yet the diagnostic power reverses.
123	Full IRT parameterization is unnecessary for mere detection, but the value of $\ell_z^*$ lies in three capabilities that HT and $z$-scores lack:
124	(a) \emph{seen/unseen decomposition}: $\ell_z^*$ can be computed separately on seen and unseen item subsets, though item-level detection is near-random (AUROC $\approx 0.53$; Appendix~\ref{app:item_auroc}), confirming that the contamination signal is diffuse and requires model-level aggregation;
125	(b) \emph{$\theta$-shift mechanism}: the ability parameter exposes why detection sensitivity depends on model ability (\S\ref{sec:theta_dynamics}), a mechanistic insight inaccessible to non-parametric statistics;
126	(c) \emph{structural sensitivity}: on real leaderboard data, $\ell_z^*$ flags 57/60 model-benchmark cells as aberrant---evidence of systematic IRT assumption violations that motivates the $\Delta\ell_z^*$ matched-difference design (\S\ref{sec:did}; Appendix~\ref{app:leaderboard_aberrance}).
127	Accuracy $z$-scores flag only 4/60 cells, making them insensitive to the response-pattern structure that $\ell_z^*$ exploits for within-model diagnosis.
128	While such patterns have theoretical antecedents in person-fit literature \citep{stonge2011}, the specific magnitude and model-dependence we observe are new empirical findings in the LLM domain; nonparametric alternatives \citep{tendeiro2014} may complement $\ell_z^*$ where 4PL calibration is unavailable.
129	
130	In practice, a two-stage workflow follows: screen using accuracy $z$-scores (Table~\ref{tab:degradation}), then apply $\ell_z^*$ to characterize whether the signal reflects $\theta$-shift absorption (indicating fixed-$\theta$ anchoring is needed) or uniform aberrance (suggesting direct memorization).
131	
132	Within the IRT family, the 4PL specification matters: simulation ablations show a mean $+$27.3pp power gain over 3PL on MMLU, because 46\% of MMLU items have upper asymptote $d < 0.95$, and the 3PL model (which assumes $d{=}1$) misattributes slip-related response patterns as aberrance (Appendix~\ref{app:4pl_ablation}).

159	\subsection{Ability-Dependent Non-Monotonic Dose-Response}
160	\label{sec:inverted_u}
161	
162	As an exploratory observation, the free-$\theta$ dose-response is non-monotonic for Qwen.

167

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Detection Signal Across Model Families}
\label{sec:detection}

Table~\ref{tab:cohens_d} presents Cohen's $d$ effect sizes for $\ell_z^*$ across three model families and two benchmarks.
All confidence intervals exclude zero, confirming that $\Delta\ell_z^*$ reliably separates contaminated from clean models at both contamination levels.

On MMLU, effect sizes range from $|d|{=}1.99$ (Llama at 25\%) to $|d|{=}7.44$ (Qwen at 25\%), with Qwen at 5\% ($|d|{=}4.15$) confirming detection at the lowest contamination level tested. Llama ($|d|{=}2.11$/$1.99$/$2.33$) and Mistral ($|d|{=}3.01$/$3.50$) show comparable magnitudes.
On ARC-C (295 items), Qwen yields $|d|{=}3.16$ at 15\% and $|d|{=}5.30$ at 50\%, demonstrating that detection remains feasible even on small benchmarks when contamination is sufficiently concentrated.

Clean-model $\ell_z^*$ baselines diverge substantially across families: Qwen ${+}8.68$ ($\text{SD}{=}0.74$), Mistral ${+}4.02$ ($\text{SD}{=}2.05$), Llama ${+}0.26$ ($\text{SD}{=}1.54$), and ARC-C Qwen ${-}5.42$ ($\text{SD}{=}0.16$).
Absolute $\ell_z^*$ thresholds would produce contradictory results: Qwen's contaminated $\ell_z^*$ at 15\% (${+}3.8$) is still positive.
The $\Delta\ell_z^*$ design normalizes these divergent baselines: Cohen's $d$ yields comparable effect sizes ($|d|{=}1.99$--$7.44$) despite order-of-magnitude differences.
Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} provides a visual summary.

\subsection{Model-Specific $\theta$-Shift Dynamics}
\label{sec:theta_dynamics}

The cross-family variation in Table~\ref{tab:cohens_d}---Qwen's $|d|$ declining from 25\% to 50\% while Llama's remains flat---suggests detection sensitivity depends on more than contamination dose.
Contamination raises overall accuracy, which inflates $\hat{\theta}_{\text{MLE}}$; a higher $\hat{\theta}$ ``explains away'' anomalous successes on hard items, absorbing the contamination signal into the ability estimate.
We term this \emph{$\theta$-shift absorption}.
The magnitude of $\theta$-shift is comparable across families---Qwen ($\Delta\theta{=}0.47$ at 50\%) and Llama ($\Delta\theta{=}0.52$)---yet their fixed-$\theta$ amplification diverges markedly (Table~\ref{tab:theta_fixed}), indicating that $\theta$-shift magnitude alone does not predict fixed-$\theta$ benefit.
Figure~\ref{fig:theta_scatter} plots baseline accuracy against Cohen's $|d|$ for all model-benchmark combinations.

$\theta$-shift absorption is the dominant source of detection variability for high-ability models at high contamination:
(i) fixed-$\theta$ estimation amplifies Qwen's multi-seed $|d|$ by 2.4$\times$ at 50\% ($5.08 \to 12.32$; Table~\ref{tab:theta_fixed}), while Llama shows no amplification ($0.4\times$);
(ii) $\theta$-anchoring reduces Qwen's inter-seed CV from 60\% to 19\%, confirming that training-run variance is driven by $\theta$-shift stochasticity rather than true signal variance;
(iii) the cross-model ranking under free-$\theta$ is seed-dependent at 50\%, making $\theta$-anchoring a necessary condition for reliable detection of high-ability models at high contamination.

ARC-C reverses this pattern.
Despite Qwen's high baseline accuracy on ARC-C (89.7\%), contamination produces larger, not smaller, effect sizes ($|d|{=}3.16$ at 15\%, $|d|{=}5.30$ at 50\%).
This reversal reflects a ceiling effect: with only 295 items and 89.7\% baseline accuracy, the already-correct items offer minimal room for further $\theta$ inflation, so contamination manifests primarily as anomalous successes on the few remaining hard items.
The small item count amplifies this concentration, producing a disproportionately large $\ell_z^*$ shift per contaminated item.

The baseline $\ell_z^*$ for ARC-C is negative ($-5.42$), reflecting the 4PL model's expectation of near-perfect performance; contamination pushes $\ell_z^*$ toward zero, producing the positive Cohen's $d$ values in Table~\ref{tab:cohens_d}.

These findings indicate that detection sensitivity is not a fixed property of $\ell_z^*$ but depends on the interaction between model ability and benchmark characteristics, a consideration absent from standard person-fit applications.

\paragraph{Fixed-$\theta$ estimation.}
Table~\ref{tab:theta_fixed} compares free-$\theta$ and fixed-$\theta$ Cohen's $d$ across all three families.
The benefit of fixed-$\theta$ is modulated by baseline $\ell_z^*$ level rather than $\theta$-shift magnitude.
Qwen (67.8\% accuracy, $\Delta\theta{=}0.47$, baseline $\ell_z^*{=}{+}8.68$) shows 2.4$\times$ amplification at 50\%: its large baseline departure from the IRT null provides substantial signal that free-$\theta$ absorption erodes, which $\theta$-anchoring recovers (multi-seed mean ${\ell_z^*}_{\text{fixed}} {=} 14.5$ vs.\ clean $7.35$).
Mistral (52.4\%, baseline $\ell_z^*{=}{+}4.02$) shows 1.7$\times$ at 50\%.
Llama (59.4\%, $\Delta\theta{=}0.39$ at 15\%, $0.52$ at 50\%) shows 0.4$\times$ at 50\% despite comparable $\theta$-shift: its near-zero baseline $\ell_z^*$ ($+0.26$) indicates that the clean response pattern conforms to IRT expectations, leaving no absorbed signal for $\theta$-anchoring to recover.
The amplification ratio tracks baseline $|\ell_z^*|$ monotonically ($8.68 {\to} 2.4{\times}$; $4.02 {\to} 1.7{\times}$; $0.26 {\to} 0.4{\times}$ at 50\%), making fixed-$\theta$ a targeted remedy for models with substantial baseline misfit, not a universal one.

  \label{fig:theta_scatter}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Detection-Diagnosis Tradeoff}
\label{sec:degradation}

Having established that $\theta$-shift complicates detection, we ask whether the full 4PL framework is necessary, or whether simpler statistics suffice.
Table~\ref{tab:degradation} compares three statistics at decreasing levels of information access: $\ell_z^*$ (requires 4PL parameters $a, b, c, d$), the HT statistic (requires only difficulty $b$), and an accuracy $z$-score (requires no item parameters).

The comparison reveals a detection-diagnosis tradeoff.
For pure detection, simpler statistics are more powerful: accuracy $z$-scores yield $|d|$ values several-fold to over an order of magnitude larger than person-fit statistics (Table~\ref{tab:degradation}), because cross-seed accuracy variance is near-zero in controlled settings.
HT generally exceeds $\ell_z^*$ in detection strength, since HT is not attenuated by the Snijders correction for $\theta$ estimation uncertainty.
Both person-fit statistics exhibit seed-dependent non-monotonicity under free-$\theta$ estimation (Table~\ref{tab:degradation}), confirming that $\theta$-shift absorption affects all statistics conditioned on ability, not $\ell_z^*$ specifically.

Yet the diagnostic power reverses.
Full IRT parameterization is unnecessary for mere detection, but the value of $\ell_z^*$ lies in three capabilities that HT and $z$-scores lack:
(a) \emph{seen/unseen decomposition}: $\ell_z^*$ can be computed separately on seen and unseen item subsets, though item-level detection is near-random (AUROC $\approx 0.53$; Appendix~\ref{app:item_auroc}), confirming that the contamination signal is diffuse and requires model-level aggregation;
(b) \emph{$\theta$-shift mechanism}: the ability parameter exposes why detection sensitivity depends on model ability (\S\ref{sec:theta_dynamics}), a mechanistic insight inaccessible to non-parametric statistics;
(c) \emph{structural sensitivity}: on real leaderboard data, $\ell_z^*$ flags 57/60 model-benchmark cells as aberrant---evidence of systematic IRT assumption violations that motivates the $\Delta\ell_z^*$ matched-difference design (\S\ref{sec:did}; Appendix~\ref{app:leaderboard_aberrance}).
Accuracy $z$-scores flag only 4/60 cells, making them insensitive to the response-pattern structure that $\ell_z^*$ exploits for within-model diagnosis.
While such patterns have theoretical antecedents in person-fit literature \citep{stonge2011}, the specific magnitude and model-dependence we observe are new empirical findings in the LLM domain; nonparametric alternatives \citep{tendeiro2014} may complement $\ell_z^*$ where 4PL calibration is unavailable.

In practice, a two-stage workflow follows: screen using accuracy $z$-scores (Table~\ref{tab:degradation}), then apply $\ell_z^*$ to characterize whether the signal reflects $\theta$-shift absorption (indicating fixed-$\theta$ anchoring is needed) or uniform aberrance (suggesting direct memorization).

Within the IRT family, the 4PL specification matters: simulation ablations show a mean $+$27.3pp power gain over 3PL on MMLU, because 46\% of MMLU items have upper asymptote $d < 0.95$, and the 3PL model (which assumes $d{=}1$) misattributes slip-related response patterns as aberrance (Appendix~\ref{app:4pl_ablation}).

\subsection{Ability-Dependent Non-Monotonic Dose-Response}
\label{sec:inverted_u}

As an exploratory observation, the free-$\theta$ dose-response is non-monotonic for Qwen.
The multi-seed mean trajectory ($|d|$: $4.15 \to 5.36 \to 7.44 \to 5.08$ at 5\%/15\%/25\%/50\%; Appendix~\ref{app:reproducibility}) shows signal peaking at 25\% before declining at 50\%, but the decline is attenuated relative to single-seed estimates and the inter-seed variance at 50\% is high (CV${=}$60\%, range $[1.90, 7.91]$).
This non-monotonicity is a $\theta$-estimation artifact: fixed-$\theta$ analysis eliminates the inverted-U and reveals a strong positive dose-response (mean $|d|$: $5.89$ at 25\% vs.\ $12.32$ at 50\%, no seed-level overlap), while reducing the 50\% CV to 19\%.
Llama shows an approximately flat dose-response ($|d|{=}2.11 \to 1.99 \to 2.33$), consistent with its near-zero $\ell_z^*$ baseline ($+0.26$ vs.\ ${+}8.68$ for Qwen) despite comparable $\theta$-shift ($\Delta\theta{=}0.52$ vs.\ $0.47$).
The mechanism is predictable from simulation (Appendix~\ref{app:simulation}): at moderate contamination, aberrant responses dominate; at high contamination, inflated $\hat{\theta}$ absorbs the anomaly---but the magnitude is highly seed-dependent.

A simulated power analysis corroborates these findings: two-sided testing (flagging both large negative and large positive $\ell_z^*$) achieves ${>}$93\% power on MMLU at all contamination levels, with the theoretical power function yielding $R^2 {=} 0.957$ against simulated values (Appendix~\ref{app:simulation}).

119	\midrule
120	15\% contam. & $-$3.42 & $-$2.95 & 0.47 & Yes \\
121	50\% contam. & $-$0.99 & $-$3.31 & 2.32 & Yes \\

123	\end{tabular}
124	\end{table}
125	
126	\section{Baseline $\ell_z^*$ Interpretation}
127	\label{app:baseline_meaning}
128	
129	The baseline $\ell_z^*$ value reflects a model's difficulty-ordering consistency under the 4PL model, not its accuracy alone.
130	In the PSN-IRT leaderboard data (12 models $\times$ 5 benchmarks, distinct from our controlled experiments), Mistral ($\text{acc}{=}0.514$, lowest among the 12 models) exhibits $\ell_z^*{=}{+}5.42$ (second highest), because its response pattern follows the IRT-predicted difficulty ordering more closely than higher-accuracy models whose responses violate the assumed item structure.
131	This dissociation explains why Mistral produces the strongest contamination signal despite the lowest accuracy: its lower baseline ability ($\hat{\theta}{=}{-}1.16$) provides greater $\theta$-shift headroom.
132	
133	\section{Leaderboard Aberrance Analysis}
134	\label{app:leaderboard_aberrance}
135	
136	We computed $\ell_z^*$ and accuracy $z$-scores for all 12 models $\times$ 5 benchmarks $=$ 60 cells in the PSN-IRT leaderboard dataset.
137	Using the standard $|\ell_z^*| > 1.96$ threshold ($\alpha{=}0.05$, two-tailed), 57 of 60 cells are flagged as aberrant, indicating pervasive IRT assumption violations in production LLM responses.
138	In contrast, accuracy $z$-scores ($|z| > 1.96$) flag only 4 of 60 cells.
139	This stark asymmetry---95\% aberrance by $\ell_z^*$ versus 7\% by accuracy---motivates the $\Delta\ell_z^*$ matched-difference design (\S\ref{sec:did}), which sidesteps absolute thresholds by comparing each model against its own clean baseline.
140	
141	\section{Item-Level Detection Results}
142	\label{app:item_auroc}
143	
144	Table~\ref{tab:item_auroc} reports item-level contamination detection performance at 15\% contamination on MMLU.
145	All methods perform near random (AUROC $\leq 0.63$), confirming that contamination is diffuse across the response pattern and that model-level aggregation via $\ell_z^*$ is essential.
146	
147	An accuracy $z$-score baseline yields $z{=}160$ at 15\% contamination, but this reflects near-zero cross-seed accuracy variance ($\text{std}{=}0.0003$), not genuine discriminability.
148	In deployment, accuracy variability from prompt format, evaluation harness, and hardware differences inflates the denominator, collapsing the $z$-score.
149	
150	\begin{table}[t]
151	\centering
152	\caption{Item-level contamination detection (AUROC) at 15\% contamination on MMLU.}
153	\label{tab:item_auroc}
154	\footnotesize
155	\begin{tabular}{@{}lc@{}}
156	\toprule
157	Method & AUROC \\
158	\midrule
159	Random baseline & 0.50 \\
160	$\ell_z^*$ itemwise & 0.53 \\
161	LR cross-model & 0.59 \\
162	RF cross-model & 0.63 \\
163	\bottomrule
164	\end{tabular}
165	\end{table}

167	\section{Robustness Analysis}
168	\label{app:robustness}
169	
170	\subsection{$\Delta\ell_z^*$ Under Local Dependence}
171	\label{app:local_dep}
172	
173	IRT person-fit statistics assume local independence---conditional on $\theta$, item responses are independent.
174	LLM benchmarks violate this assumption through topical clustering (e.g., MMLU subjects); resampling-based approaches can provide valid person-fit assessment even under such violations \citep{sinharay2016}.
175	We evaluate whether the $\Delta\ell_z^*$ matched-difference design is robust to local dependence (LD) via two simulation scenarios on 14,042 MMLU items with 1,000 replications each.
176	
177	\paragraph{Shared LD.}
178	Clean and contaminated conditions share identical testlet structure (${\sim}200$ testlets of ${\sim}70$ items, random effect $\gamma_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_\tau)$).
179	Table~\ref{tab:ld_shared} reports absolute $\ell_z^*$ Type~I error and the ratio of $\Delta\ell_z^*$ effect size ($d$) to the no-LD baseline.
180	While absolute $\ell_z^*$ Type~I error inflates severely under LD (0.043$\to$0.939 at $\sigma{=}1.0$), the $\Delta\ell_z^*$ design maintains detection power: $d_{\text{ratio}} \geq 0.93$ for $\sigma_\tau \leq 0.5$ (realistic range), confirming that shared misfit is cancelled by the matched-difference design.
181	
182	\begin{table}[t]
183	\centering
184	\caption{Robustness of $\Delta\ell_z^*$ to shared local dependence (1,000 replications, MMLU). $d_{\text{ratio}}$: effect size relative to the $\sigma_\tau{=}0$ baseline.}
185	\label{tab:ld_shared}
186	\footnotesize
187	\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
188	\toprule
189	$\sigma_\tau$ & Abs.\ $\ell_z^*$ Type~I & $d_{\text{ratio}}$ (15\%) & $d_{\text{ratio}}$ (50\%) \\
190	\midrule
191	0.0 & 0.043 & 1.000 & 1.000 \\
192	0.3 & 0.110 & 1.002 & 1.038 \\
193	0.5 & 0.454 & 0.934 & 1.028 \\
194	1.0 & 0.939 & 0.705 & 1.061 \\
195	\bottomrule
196	\end{tabular}
197	\end{table}
198	
199	\paragraph{Asymmetric LD.}
200	In the second scenario, contaminated models' seen items share an additional memory factor ($\gamma_{\text{mem}} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_{\text{mem}})$), simulating contamination-specific LD not present in clean conditions ($\sigma_\tau{=}0.5$ fixed).
201	Table~\ref{tab:ld_asym} shows that $\Delta\ell_z^*$ maintains ${\geq}98.5\%$ power across all conditions, even when contamination introduces asymmetric dependence among seen items.
202	
203	\begin{table}[t]
204	\centering
205	\caption{$\Delta\ell_z^*$ detection under asymmetric local dependence ($\sigma_\tau{=}0.5$, contamination-specific memory factor $\sigma_{\text{mem}}$; 1,000 replications, MMLU).}
206	\label{tab:ld_asym}
207	\footnotesize
208	\begin{tabular}{@{}lcccc@{}}
209	\toprule
210	$\sigma_{\text{mem}}$ & Power (15\%) & $d$ (15\%) & Power (50\%) & $d$ (50\%) \\
211	\midrule
212	0.5 & 0.987 & $-$2.107 & 0.991 & $-$2.337 \\
213	1.0 & 0.993 & $-$2.104 & 0.985 & $-$1.587 \\
214	\bottomrule
215	\end{tabular}
216	\end{table}
217	
218	\subsection{Sensitivity to Item Parameter Estimation Error}
219	\label{app:param_perturb}
220	
221	PSN-IRT item parameters carry estimation error from the calibration sample.
222	We evaluate detection sensitivity by adding joint noise to all four parameters: multiplicative perturbation $p' = p \cdot (1 + \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma))$ for $a$, $c$, and $d$; additive perturbation $b' = b + \sigma \cdot \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ for difficulty.
223	Tables~\ref{tab:param_noise_free} and \ref{tab:param_noise_fixed} report results over 100 trials using Qwen MMLU response vectors.
224	
225	Detection of 15\% contamination is robust to parameter noise under free-$\theta$ (17.4\% bias at $\sigma{=}10\%$, $|d|$ still ${>}5$; Table~\ref{tab:param_noise_free}).
226	The 50\% contamination condition under free-$\theta$ is fragile---consistent with its already-weak signal due to $\theta$-shift absorption (\S\ref{sec:inverted_u}).
227	
228	Under $\theta$-fixed estimation (Table~\ref{tab:param_noise_fixed}), detection is highly robust: 10\% perturbation produces ${<}4\%$ bias in Cohen's $d$, with worst-case $|d| = 3.73$ (15\% contamination) and $12.20$ (50\%)---both far exceeding conventional thresholds.
229	This contrasts sharply with free-$\theta$ estimation, where 50\% contamination Cohen's $d$ collapses to near zero under 10\% noise.
230	The complementarity is clear: conditions where free-$\theta$ detection is fragile (high-baseline-accuracy models with $\theta$-shift absorption) are precisely where $\theta$-fixed anchoring provides the strongest and most noise-robust signal.
231

265	\section{BCa Bootstrap Sensitivity Check}
266	\label{app:bca}
267	
268	As a sensitivity check, we computed bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) bootstrap confidence intervals for all Cohen's $d$ estimates.
269	BCa CIs were uniformly narrower than the percentile CIs reported in the main text (mean reduction 22\%), confirming that our reported intervals are conservative.
270	The single condition where BCa widens the zero-crossing set---Llama fixed-$\theta$ at 50\% contamination, BCa CI [$-$0.13, 2.21] vs.\ percentile CI [0.17, 2.97]---is already characterized as ineffective in \S\ref{sec:theta_dynamics}.
271	
272	\section{Classical IRT Refit from Leaderboard Data}
273	\label{app:mml_em}
274	
275	To assess whether item parameters can be recovered without PSN-IRT's neural calibration, we applied classical MML-EM estimation (Gauss--Hermite quadrature, $Q{=}31$ nodes) to binary response data from $N{=}178$ models on the Open LLM Leaderboard v1.
276	With 14,042 MMLU items and an examinee-to-item ratio of $N{:}J = 0.013$---far below the $N{>}500$ typically required for stable 3PL estimation---discrimination parameters are severely under-determined.
277	
278	Table~\ref{tab:mml_em} reports parameter correlations between MML-EM-fitted and PSN-IRT parameters.
279	Difficulty shows moderate agreement ($r_b{=}0.663$), but discrimination is essentially unrecovered ($r_a{=}0.127$).
280	Using these MML-EM parameters produces miscalibrated $\ell_z^*$ statistics (mean$\,{=}\,$11.2, expected ${\approx}\,$0), confirming that the refitted model does not capture the data-generating process.
281	This motivates the dependence on PSN-IRT's externally calibrated item bank (\S\ref{sec:framework}).

300	\section{Post-RL Preliminary Observation}
301	\label{app:post_rl}
302	
303	\citet{wang2025fragility} show that all MIA-based detectors fail after RL post-training.
304	In a single-model pilot ($N{=}1$, Qwen, GRPO), we applied GRPO \citep{shao2024} for 1,500 steps to a contaminated model (15\% MMLU) and evaluated at three checkpoints.
305	GRPO erases the accuracy gap between seen and unseen items ($11.4\text{pp} \to 2.1\text{pp}$), but the $\ell_z^*$ response-pattern gap persists (${\sim}3.3$; Figure~\ref{fig:grpo}), suggesting structural traces of contamination may survive RL alignment.
306	Min-K\% membership inference confirms this dissociation: while SFT yields a weak MIA signal (AUC-ROC${=}0.611$), GRPO training drives AUC to $0.493$ (step~500), $0.493$ (step~1000), and $0.493$ (step~1500)---indistinguishable from random chance ($0.50$) as RL erases memorization-based features while the response-pattern anomaly that $\ell_z^*$ detects persists.
307	This $N{=}1$ observation requires validation across model families, RL methods, and contamination levels before any conclusions can be drawn.

\section*{Limitations}

Our controlled experiments cover three 7--8B model families with QLoRA fine-tuning; generalization to larger scales, mixture-of-experts architectures, full-parameter fine-tuning, and pretraining-stage contamination remains untested.
Most contamination conditions use a single training run, and multi-seed replication (available for Qwen) reveals high seed dependence at 50\% contamination (CV${=}$60\%), partially resolved by $\theta$-anchoring; the post-RL characterization is $N{=}1$.
The framework depends on pre-calibrated 4PL item parameters from PSN-IRT, whose calibration sample may include contaminated models, and we do not provide head-to-head comparison with logit-based methods (MIA, ConStat) that operate at a different information level.

1	\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}
2	
3	Our findings reveal both the strengths and boundaries of IRT person-fit for contamination detection: $\ell_z^*$ reliably detects SFT-stage contamination across model families, but three boundary conditions constrain its practical utility.
4	
5	\paragraph{Characterization over tool.}
6	The detection-diagnosis tradeoff (\S\ref{sec:degradation}) shows that simpler statistics detect contamination more powerfully than $\ell_z^*$: accuracy $z$-scores yield $|d|$ values several-fold to over an order of magnitude larger, and HT generally exceeds $\ell_z^*$.
7	The value of the IRT framework lies not in detection power but in mechanistic understanding: the $\theta$-shift analysis reveals \emph{why} detection sensitivity varies across models and contamination levels, the seen/unseen decomposition identifies \emph{what fraction} of items are memorized, and the 4PL parameterization captures item-level ceiling effects that 3PL misattributes as aberrance.
8	These diagnostic capabilities are invisible to accuracy $z$-scores or HT.
9	Findings~1--2 are theoretically predictable from IRT principles; our contribution lies in quantifying these effects in the LLM setting, where the magnitude and boundary conditions are not derivable from theory alone.
10	
11	\paragraph{Practical implications.}
12	Two results have immediate consequences.
13	Free-$\theta$ estimation produces seed-dependent dose-response curves (CV up to 60\%); anchoring $\theta$ to a pre-contamination baseline stabilizes detection and amplifies the signal for models whose clean $\ell_z^*$ departs substantially from zero.
14	The benchmark size boundary means $\ell_z^*$ is most informative for large benchmarks ($n \approx 8{,}000$ items for 80\% power at 15\% contamination); on small benchmarks like ARC-C (295 items), detection relies on concentrated contamination effects.
15	
16	\paragraph{Scope and calibration.}
17	Universal baseline misfit (57/60 cells flagged) confirms systematic IRT violations; the $\Delta\ell_z^*$ design turns this into a feature through within-model differencing.
18	PSN-IRT provides pre-calibrated 4PL parameters \citep{psnirt2026}, but classical calibration fails on contaminated data ($r_a{=}0.127$; Appendix~\ref{app:mml_em}); the calibration sample (13,000+ models) may itself include contaminated ones, though individual contamination effects are diluted across models.
19	The robustness analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:param_perturb}) provides partial reassurance (${\pm}10\%$ noise tolerance).
20	\paragraph{Information requirements and method positioning.}
21	$\ell_z^*$ sits below MIA \citep[logits;][]{minkprob2024} and ConStat \citep[multi-benchmark scores;][]{constat2024} in an information-requirements hierarchy, needing only single-benchmark binary patterns and an external item bank---suited to retrospective audits where logits are unavailable. \section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

Our findings reveal both the strengths and boundaries of IRT person-fit for contamination detection: $\ell_z^*$ reliably detects SFT-stage contamination across model families, but three boundary conditions constrain its practical utility.

\paragraph{Characterization over tool.}
The detection-diagnosis tradeoff (\S\ref{sec:degradation}) shows that simpler statistics detect contamination more powerfully than $\ell_z^*$: accuracy $z$-scores yield $|d|$ values several-fold to over an order of magnitude larger, and HT generally exceeds $\ell_z^*$.
The value of the IRT framework lies not in detection power but in mechanistic understanding: the $\theta$-shift analysis reveals \emph{why} detection sensitivity varies across models and contamination levels, the seen/unseen decomposition identifies \emph{what fraction} of items are memorized, and the 4PL parameterization captures item-level ceiling effects that 3PL misattributes as aberrance.
These diagnostic capabilities are invisible to accuracy $z$-scores or HT.
Findings~1--2 are theoretically predictable from IRT principles; our contribution lies in quantifying these effects in the LLM setting, where the magnitude and boundary conditions are not derivable from theory alone.

\paragraph{Practical implications.}
Two results have immediate consequences.
Free-$\theta$ estimation produces seed-dependent dose-response curves (CV up to 60\%); anchoring $\theta$ to a pre-contamination baseline stabilizes detection and amplifies the signal for models whose clean $\ell_z^*$ departs substantially from zero.
The benchmark size boundary means $\ell_z^*$ is most informative for large benchmarks ($n \approx 8{,}000$ items for 80\% power at 15\% contamination); on small benchmarks like ARC-C (295 items), detection relies on concentrated contamination effects.

\paragraph{Scope and calibration.}
Universal baseline misfit (57/60 cells flagged) confirms systematic IRT violations; the $\Delta\ell_z^*$ design turns this into a feature through within-model differencing.
PSN-IRT provides pre-calibrated 4PL parameters \citep{psnirt2026}, but classical calibration fails on contaminated data ($r_a{=}0.127$; Appendix~\ref{app:mml_em}); the calibration sample (13,000+ models) may itself include contaminated ones, though individual contamination effects are diluted across models.
The robustness analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:param_perturb}) provides partial reassurance (${\pm}10\%$ noise tolerance).
\paragraph{Information requirements and method positioning.}
$\ell_z^*$ sits below MIA \citep[logits;][]{minkprob2024} and ConStat \citep[multi-benchmark scores;][]{constat2024} in an information-requirements hierarchy, needing only single-benchmark binary patterns and an external item bank---suited to retrospective audits where logits are unavailable. Our GRPO pilot directly confirms this advantage: Min-K\% AUC degrades from $0.611$ (SFT) to $0.493$ (post-RL), indistinguishable from chance, while $\ell_z^*$ signal persists (${\sim}3.3$; Figure~\ref{fig:grpo}), demonstrating that response-pattern anomalies survive RL alignment that eliminates memorization-based features \citep{wang2025fragility}.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Benchmark contamination, the unintended inclusion of evaluation data in training corpora, poses a growing threat to the integrity of large language model (LLM) evaluation \citep{dodge2021, magar2022, sainz2023}.
As training corpora and public benchmarks both expand, the probability of overlap increases structurally \citep{jacovi2023, chang2024survey}.
When contamination occurs, benchmark scores no longer reflect genuine capability, undermining the primary mechanism by which the community compares and selects models.

A range of detection methods have been proposed, but all require some form of privileged access beyond the binary response record.
N-gram overlap methods need the training corpus \citep{dodge2021, magar2022}.
Membership inference approaches require token-level probabilities \citep{minkprob2024, deng2024}.
Probing methods rely on crafted prompts \citep{golchin2024, oren2024}.
Performance-based methods require multiple test variants or output logits \citep{constat2024, codec2026}.
These methods form a detection frontier ordered by information access.
No existing method operates using only binary response patterns, without model weights, gradients, logits, or training data---though, as we show, effective detection additionally requires externally calibrated item parameters.

In this work, we focus on SFT-stage contamination---where benchmark answers are explicitly included in fine-tuning data---for three reasons.
First, controlled experiments require known ground-truth contamination sets, achievable through fine-tuning with specific benchmark items.
Second, SFT-stage contamination is increasingly relevant as fine-tuning-as-a-service platforms proliferate, creating new pathways for benchmark data to enter training mixtures.
Third, SFT provides a methodologically clean setting to characterize detection boundaries before extending to noisier pretraining scenarios.

The need for detection from binary response patterns grows more pressing as models evolve.
\citet{wang2025fragility} show that all ten log-probability-based methods they evaluate perform at chance level on models trained with reinforcement learning (RL), because RL reshapes internal token distributions while preserving binary correctness patterns.
This motivates a fundamental question: \emph{what can binary response patterns reveal about contamination, and under what conditions?}

We observe that a contaminated LLM is functionally analogous to a test-taker with item preknowledge: both produce response patterns in which difficult items are answered correctly through memorization rather than genuine ability.
This connection points to person-fit statistics, developed over four decades for cheating detection in educational testing \citep{drasgow1985, meijer2001, karabatsos2003, sinharay2017}.
The standardized statistic $\ell_z^*$ \citep{snijders2001} measures how well a response pattern conforms to Item Response Theory (IRT) model predictions.
Figure~\ref{fig:motivation} illustrates this analogy.
Despite the natural correspondence, no prior work has applied person-fit statistics to LLM benchmark contamination.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig_1_response_pattern.pdf}
  \caption{A clean model's responses track the IRT-predicted probability curve (left); a contaminated model shows anomalous successes on hard items (right, red diamonds), producing a large $|\Delta\ell_z^*|$ signal.}
  \label{fig:motivation}
\end{figure}

Rather than proposing $\ell_z^*$ as a ready-to-deploy detection tool, we characterize the behavior boundaries of IRT person-fit statistics for LLM contamination detection.
Our framework operates at three layers: (i) pre-calibrated 4PL item parameters from the PSN-IRT item bank \citep{psnirt2026}, an external resource derived from 13,000+ models; (ii) binary response patterns obtained from the target model without access to weights or logits; and (iii) retrospective statistical inference requiring no model modification.
Using controlled contamination experiments across three 7--8B model families (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B; $n{=}10$ clean seeds each) with pre-calibrated 4PL item parameters from PSN-IRT \citep{psnirt2026}, we identify three IRT-specific findings on MMLU \citep{hendrycks2021mmlu} and ARC-Challenge:

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
\item \textbf{Model-specific $\theta$-shift dynamics.} Contamination inflates ability estimates ($\hat{\theta}$), absorbing the person-fit signal; $\theta$-anchoring amplifies Qwen's multi-seed $|d|$ by 2.4$\times$ at 50\% contamination while reducing inter-seed CV from 60\% to 19\%, establishing $\theta$-anchoring as a necessary condition for reliable detection of high-ability models at high contamination. ARC-C reverses through a ceiling effect.

\item \textbf{Detection-diagnosis tradeoff.} Simpler statistics yield stronger detection: accuracy $z$-scores produce $|d|$ values several-fold to over an order of magnitude larger than person-fit statistics, and HT generally exceeds $\ell_z^*$. Yet the diagnostic power reverses: only $\ell_z^*$ supports seen/unseen decomposition, mechanistic $\theta$-shift analysis, and sensitivity to response-pattern structure (57/60 vs.\ 4/60 flagged cells on real-world data).

\item \textbf{Non-monotonic dose-response under free-$\theta$ (exploratory).} Multi-seed Qwen trajectory ($|d|$: $4.15 \to 5.36 \to 7.44 \to 5.08$ at 5\%/15\%/25\%/50\%) shows attenuated non-monotonicity; $\theta$-anchoring eliminates the pattern and reveals strong positive dose-response ($|d|{=}12.32$ at 50\%). The non-monotonicity is a $\theta$-estimation artifact, not a detection boundary.
\end{enumerate}

Our contributions are threefold:
(1) We provide the first empirical characterization of IRT person-fit behavior for LLM contamination, quantifying theoretically predicted phenomena ($\theta$-shift absorption, detection-diagnosis tradeoff) whose magnitudes and boundary conditions are not derivable from IRT theory alone.
(2) We establish that $\Delta\ell_z^*$ reliably detects SFT-stage contamination across three model families (all bootstrap 95\% CIs exclude zero, $n{=}10$).
(3) We document the detection-diagnosis tradeoff, clarifying what binary response patterns can and cannot reveal.
Findings~1--2 are confirmatory (pre-planned 15\%/50\% $\times$ 3 families); Finding~3 is exploratory (5\%/25\% added post-hoc).

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

Our findings reveal both the strengths and boundaries of IRT person-fit for contamination detection: $\ell_z^*$ reliably detects SFT-stage contamination across model families, but three boundary conditions constrain its practical utility.

\paragraph{Characterization over tool.}
The detection-diagnosis tradeoff (\S\ref{sec:degradation}) shows that simpler statistics detect contamination more powerfully than $\ell_z^*$: accuracy $z$-scores yield $|d|$ values several-fold to over an order of magnitude larger, and HT generally exceeds $\ell_z^*$.
The value of the IRT framework lies not in detection power but in mechanistic understanding: the $\theta$-shift analysis reveals \emph{why} detection sensitivity varies across models and contamination levels, the seen/unseen decomposition identifies \emph{what fraction} of items are memorized, and the 4PL parameterization captures item-level ceiling effects that 3PL misattributes as aberrance.
These diagnostic capabilities are invisible to accuracy $z$-scores or HT.
Findings~1--2 are theoretically predictable from IRT principles; our contribution lies in quantifying these effects in the LLM setting, where the magnitude and boundary conditions are not derivable from theory alone.

\paragraph{Practical implications.}
Two results have immediate consequences.
Free-$\theta$ estimation produces seed-dependent dose-response curves (CV up to 60\%); anchoring $\theta$ to a pre-contamination baseline stabilizes detection and amplifies the signal for models whose clean $\ell_z^*$ departs substantially from zero.
The benchmark size boundary means $\ell_z^*$ is most informative for large benchmarks ($n \approx 8{,}000$ items for 80\% power at 15\% contamination); on small benchmarks like ARC-C (295 items), detection relies on concentrated contamination effects.

\paragraph{Scope and calibration.}
Universal baseline misfit (57/60 cells flagged) confirms systematic IRT violations; the $\Delta\ell_z^*$ design turns this into a feature through within-model differencing.
PSN-IRT provides pre-calibrated 4PL parameters \citep{psnirt2026}, but classical calibration fails on contaminated data ($r_a{=}0.127$; Appendix~\ref{app:mml_em}); the calibration sample (13,000+ models) may itself include contaminated ones, though individual contamination effects are diluted across models.
The robustness analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:param_perturb}) provides partial reassurance (${\pm}10\%$ noise tolerance).
\paragraph{Information requirements and method positioning.}
$\ell_z^*$ sits below MIA \citep[logits;][]{minkprob2024} and ConStat \citep[multi-benchmark scores;][]{constat2024} in an information-requirements hierarchy, needing only single-benchmark binary patterns and an external item bank---suited to retrospective audits where logits are unavailable. Our GRPO pilot directly confirms this advantage: Min-K\% AUC degrades from $0.611$ (SFT) to $0.493$ (post-RL), indistinguishable from chance, while $\ell_z^*$ signal persists (${\sim}3.3$; Figure~\ref{fig:grpo}), demonstrating that response-pattern anomalies survive RL alignment that eliminates memorization-based features \citep{wang2025fragility}.
